synthesis: Finite critical-line verification has two noninterchangeable channels: sign changes of a real critical-line function localize odd-order on-line zeros, while argument-principle, Backlund, or Turing-style accounting supplies an independently justified total with multiplicity. Equality of the localized count and the total upgrades sampling evidence to a bounded completeness certificate.
source_support: Bombieri explicitly compares xi sign changes with the argument-principle count N(T) and derives simplicity and critical-line location when the counts agree. Moree separates N0(T) from the all-zero count N(T), gives the theta-plus-S(T) accounting route, and records the contour and nearest-integer obstructions. Platt–Trudgian likewise pair completed-zeta sign changes with a Turing-method check that all expected zeros were counted.
nonparaphrase_operation: The comparison identifies an invariant integer interface: one representation produces localized witnesses and another compresses the whole bounded zero population into a multiplicity-aware count; matching them closes the detection gap without identifying the two methods.
limits: The conclusion is confined to the certified region and depends on rigorous evaluation, valid contour or Turing hypotheses, and boundary control. Sign changes alone miss even-multiplicity behavior and cannot exclude off-line zeros; the damaged displays and outline-level Turing description do not support reconstruction of any implementation or an unbounded RH claim.
quality_reason: All three parents support the same local-witness/global-accounting architecture, and the synthesis preserves the different counting mechanisms and their separate proof burdens rather than treating them as equivalent formulas.

synthesis: Across the three computational designs, uncertainty is made into control flow: routine cases take a cheap path, values whose sign is not certified trigger local refinement or a more accurate method, runs of failures become Gram blocks, and cases still unresolved by automation are preserved for later inspection rather than silently counted as successes.
source_support: The 1956 account compares an approximate value with a remainder estimate, emits separate uncertainty and failure flags, subdivides exceptional intervals, and leaves one low maximum unresolved by that approximation. The 1982 program records a message and plot before provisional continuation and later manual inspection; it also tries shifted arguments before its expensive method and warns that the resulting statistics are not strictly accumulable with exact-Gram-point statistics. Pugh routes ordinary Gram-law successes directly to the count, packages failures into Gram blocks, and performs a second, more accurate Z evaluation only when the rough test misses its tolerance.
nonparaphrase_operation: Error margins and failed local expectations are treated as branching predicates that change the representation of the task—from point sign, to refined mesh, to bounded block, to preserved exception—while retaining provenance about which observable and method produced each decision.
limits: This adaptive routing supplies local lower-bound evidence, not the independent total needed for completeness. The 1982 manual judgments and cited closing theorem are not reproduced, provisional continuation is not certification, shifted samples change the statistic, and no parent proves that these fallbacks resolve every future exceptional block.
quality_reason: The relation is supported by explicit decision paths in every parent and yields a concrete exception-preserving search pattern; it does not erase the material mismatch between certified remainder tests, shifted sampling, manual inspection, and delegated block search.

synthesis: Both arguments make a global inequality tractable by partitioning it where different representations are strongest. The Lehmer-pair calculation bounds a finite ordered block from adjacent gaps and controls remote inverse-square mass by zero counts and decay before aggregating component bounds; the zero-free-region calculation splits a whole-line integral at branch changes and around a moving peak, using bounded numerical pieces and analytic tail majorants.
source_support: The Lehmer source bins distant ordinates, applies a local zero-count bound, and compares the weighted series with an integral; it bounds the large finite block through the nearest outer gaps and later adds the component estimates to certify the gap-interaction inequality. The zero-free-region source uses symmetry, the piecewise U0 majorant, numerical central integrals, logarithmic tail domination, and an epsilon-split around b to bound C41 and hence the relevant C4 contribution.
nonparaphrase_operation: The shared operation is domain-to-obligation routing: explicit breakpoints convert one global expression into subexpressions with compatible proof methods, after which additive structure recombines one-sided bounds into the required scalar test.
limits: The certified quantities are different and the decompositions are not interchangeable. The Lehmer calculation inherits the Lambda<0 real/simple-zero hypothesis and reported ordinate data; the integral calculation depends on its own majorant, parameters, and numerical middle-piece control. OCR-sensitive formulas, omitted interval logs, constants, endpoints, and error budgets require original-source verification, and neither certificate proves global RH or supplies a universal optimal partition.
quality_reason: The comparison is concrete at the level of additive decomposition, representation-specific bounding, and recombination. It preserves the incompatible hypotheses and targets, avoiding a generic claim that every numerical proof is merely finite-plus-tail splitting.

synthesis: The search trajectory is not itself the certificate. In the Jensen-polynomial work, approximate root discovery becomes proof-relevant only through a controlled coefficient-to-root transfer or a justified real-root count; in the trigonometric-polynomial work, annealing proposes a fixed coefficient vector whose admissibility and objective inequalities could serve as the finite upper-bound witness once independently verified.
source_support: The earlier Jensen method computes all roots and invokes an Ostrowski perturbation theorem to transfer a numerical non-real root to the exact polynomial. The later continuation search uses Sturm counts as its primary decision channel, adapts the interval and precision when counts look deficient, and retains a computed complex root only as an extra check. The degree-40 source reports a refined annealing result, a fixed polynomial, coefficient locations, and an improved objective value, while leaving the coefficient-level and rounding evidence outside the prose span.
nonparaphrase_operation: The comparison changes the evidential object from an optimizer or continuation history to a finite predicate-bearing object: controlled exact-polynomial root information on one side and an explicit admissible polynomial with a one-sided objective inequality on the other.
limits: The predicates and verification methods are different: Sturm counting does not certify trigonometric nonnegativity or its objective, and annealing does not certify polynomial root counts. The packet omits the Ostrowski hypotheses, rigorous endpoint-sign error control, and full coefficient-and-rounding verification; the restored count pattern and extra complex zero are diagnostics, not substitutes. Neither search establishes global optimality.
quality_reason: Each source supports the discovery-versus-verification distinction and a concrete finite object, while the synthesis makes the incompleteness of the available checks explicit rather than overstating either reported computation as independently replayable certification.

synthesis: The sources use three non-equivalent normalizations to ask progressively broader questions about close zeros: division by local mean spacing makes one observed gap comparable across height; the product of squared gap and inverse-square interaction tests the pair against its full zero environment; and a convex potential of reference-normalized gaps aggregates deviations to support a population-level contradiction with positive-density small gaps.
source_support: The 1986 account divides its closest observed gap by the natural local spacing and reports a scale-free value. The Lehmer definition combines the consecutive gap with a sum over all other signed zeros, and the later component aggregation verifies the resulting inequality for one pair under Lambda<0. Rodgers–Tao bound an average of the potential V at reference-normalized consecutive gaps, derive concentration near unit spacing for density one, and contradict a cited positive proportion of gaps uniformly below mean spacing.
nonparaphrase_operation: Normalization quotients out nuisance scale while retaining different levels of structure: raw local geometry becomes a height-comparable statistic, then a local-versus-global interaction scalar, then an aggregate defect whose small average has distributional consequences.
limits: These are not successive implications or interchangeable certificates. One tiny normalized gap is only a local observation; a Lehmer certificate requires consecutiveness, simplicity, the Lambda<0 branch, and full environmental control; the Rodgers–Tao step is asymptotic and population-level and relies on an external small-gap theorem. None of the three alone proves Lambda=0 or RH, and formula-level reuse remains scan-sensitive.
quality_reason: Every rung is tied to an explicit normalization and a distinct inference supported by its parent. The synthesis avoids treating visual rarity, a one-pair Lehmer inequality, and a density contradiction as equivalent evidence.

synthesis: Both analyses view heat-deformed zeros through inverse-square interaction, but they compress the environment at different scales. The close-pair method subtracts two zero velocities to obtain a gap ODE with a singular pair term and a scalar environmental correction; the many-body method localizes to finite subsystems, exposes cross-boundary terms, subtracts a reference lattice through a convex defect, and justifies an asymptotic dissipation identity for a localized Hamiltonian.
source_support: Csordas–Smith–Varga derive zero velocities from the Hadamard product, obtain the adjacent-gap equation and positive environmental term, and show in the example that the squared gap controls the leading threshold scale while the environmental bound remains necessary. Rodgers–Tao give finite-subsystem identities whose sign defects are exterior cross terms, define a nonnegative reference-normalized energy, and prove absolute continuity and almost-everywhere differentiation leading to the stated minus-four-energy main term with negligible errors.
nonparaphrase_operation: The relation tracks two reductions of the same interaction law: many external particles are first compressed to a scalar for one collision coordinate, whereas the infinite-system treatment turns environmental influence into explicit boundary errors and subtracts equilibrium so deviations become summable and differentiable.
limits: The pair-conditioned ODE and the renormalized global contradiction are not derivations of one another. Both require regimes of real simple zeros, while the infinite argument additionally needs localization, gap bounds, integrated-energy domination, and later near/far cancellation. The dissipation statement is almost everywhere and asymptotic, not exact monotonicity, and OCR damage prevents formula-exact transfer from the older source.
quality_reason: The common inverse-square dynamics and the distinct environmental treatments are explicit in all five parents. The synthesis preserves their scale, hypothesis, and proof-burden mismatch instead of promoting the pair approximation to an infinite-system theorem.

synthesis: A finite verification can be exported as a compact bounded predicate—such as RH through height H or RH for a stated modulus-height family of Dirichlet L-functions—so a later analytic argument can consume the certified range without treating the underlying zero list as the theorem. The downstream effect depends on the consumer and may be a slight constant improvement, a rigorously delimited input to an unconditional proof, or a threshold-triggered bound.
source_support: The 1986 source notes that literature consequences are parameterized by a finite verified height A but does not trace them. Moree states that Helfgott used Platt's bounded interval-arithmetic verification for a family of Dirichlet L-functions while separately improving the major- and minor-arc analysis. Platt–Trudgian identify H as an input to explicit prime estimates and show that crossing a published H cutoff yields Lambda at most 0.2 while the next cutoff remains unmet.
nonparaphrase_operation: The interface forgets individual zero coordinates while preserving the quantified range predicate required by a consuming theorem; proof reuse becomes substitution of a stronger certified bound into an independently specified analytic dependency or threshold.
limits: The zeta and Dirichlet-L certificates, ranges, and consuming theorems are not substitutable. Moree does not expose the exact interface inside Helfgott's proof, the 1986 consequences are untraced, and the prime-estimate constants are not recalculated here. Gains can be discontinuous or slight, still require all analytic hypotheses, and no bounded verification becomes global RH.
quality_reason: The modular bounded-input relation is explicit across the parents once H is generalized cautiously to a bounded family predicate. The synthesis retains the source-specific consumers and does not invent a common theorem or a proportional improvement law.

synthesis: The computational chain removes information in stages aligned with the finite certificate: a nonzero phase converts critical-line zeta values to a real Z function without moving zeros, the Riemann–Siegel representation evaluates that real amplitude with roughly square-root-many terms plus a remainder, and a count-oriented run retains certified sign-change events rather than high-precision zero coordinates.
source_support: The 1956 source defines a real phase-adjusted function, gives a short Riemann–Siegel expansion with a remainder estimate, and records close-root cases whose small intervening extrema required a fine mesh. Pugh separately explains the square-root-versus-order-t cost trade, eventual floating-point limitation, and the phase bridge from zeta to real Z sign changes. Platt–Trudgian explicitly stop after a sign change, count the zero, and omit high-precision isolation to save time and storage.
nonparaphrase_operation: Phase normalization preserves zero location while exposing order and sign; asymptotic truncation compresses evaluation subject to an error bound; event counting then preserves the local existence witness needed by global accounting while deliberately forgetting the coordinate.
limits: The chain addresses critical-line detection, not completeness: an independent multiplicity-aware total is still required, off-line zeros are invisible to this representation, and sign changes alone need not reveal even-multiplicity zeros. Short sums require certified remainder and precision control, close roots create small sign margins that may demand finer evaluation, and all conclusions remain finite.
quality_reason: All five parents support successive, goal-directed reductions with explicit information retained and lost. The synthesis does not claim that speed or sign-only storage proves completeness and keeps the numerical conditioning and separate-accounting burdens visible.
